# Week 1 - Day 1 - Fundamentals - Why automation, why Playwright

Software testing means checking that an application works the way it should. This lesson explains
what testing is, how automated testing differs from testing by hand, and why this course uses a
tool called Playwright.

| | |
|---|---|
| **Focus** | An orientation to test automation, with one guided look at the Playwright website. |
| **Goals** | Explain what automation cannot do, why teams choose Playwright over Selenium, and where automation effort is spent. |
| **Prerequisites** | No prior knowledge is required. This is the first lesson in the course. |
| **Key takeaway** | Automation does not find defects. It reports whether each check passed or failed. |

## What software testing is

An **application** is a program that people use, such as a banking website or a shopping app.
Before an application is released, someone must check that it works. That work is called
**software testing**.

A tester works from a **test case**: a list of steps, and the result those steps should produce,
which is called the **expected result**. The result you see when you follow the steps is the
**actual result**. When the two are different, the tester has found a **bug**,
which is also called a **defect**.

| Part of a test case | Example |
|---|---|
| Steps | Open the login page, enter a valid email and password, and select **Login**. |
| Expected result | The account dashboard opens. |
| Actual result | An error message appears. |
| Outcome | The actual result is different from the expected result, so this is a bug. |

## Manual testing and automated testing

In **manual testing**, a person follows the steps of a test case and decides whether the result
is correct.

In **automated testing**, a program follows the same steps. The steps and checks of a test case,
written so that a computer can follow them, are a **test script**, or a test for short. You write
the script once, and a computer can then run it as often as you need.

| | Manual testing | Automated testing |
|---|---|---|
| Who follows the steps | A person | A test script |
| Who decides whether the result is correct | The person, using their judgment | The script only compares the actual result with the expected result it was given. |
| Can it notice a problem that nobody planned to check? | Yes. A person can see that something looks wrong. | No. It checks only what it was told to check. |
| Best suited to | Exploring a new feature for the first time | Repeating the same checks many times, for example every night |
| Cost of each run | High, because it uses a person's time | Very low, once the script is written |

This leads to the most important idea in this lesson.

> **Important:** **Automation does not find bugs.** It reports whether each check **passed** or
> **failed**. When a check fails, a person investigates and decides whether the failure is a bug.

## What you need before you automate a test

You need two things before you can automate a test:

1. **A known expected result.** You must know what the correct result looks like. Otherwise, the
   script has nothing to compare the actual result with.
2. **A way to find the element.** An **element** is one item on a web page, such as a button, a
   text field, or a link. The script must be able to find the element reliably every time, so
   that it can click it, type into it, or read it.

If either one is missing, the test cannot be automated. This is why some testing, such as exploring
a new feature without a fixed goal, stays manual.

## What Playwright is

**Playwright** is a free, open-source tool, made by Microsoft, for the automated testing of web
applications. **Open-source** means that anyone can read and use its code.

Playwright controls a **web browser**, the program you use to visit websites, in the same way a
person does. It opens pages, clicks buttons, and types text. Because it uses the application the way
a user does, from the first step of a task to the last, Playwright is called an **end-to-end
testing** tool. An end-to-end test checks a complete task, such as signing in and viewing an
account balance.

Playwright works with the three main browser engines. A **browser engine** is the part of a browser
that displays web pages.

| Engine | Used by |
|---|---|
| Chromium | Google Chrome and Microsoft Edge |
| Firefox | Mozilla Firefox |
| WebKit | Apple Safari |

You write Playwright tests in a **programming language**: a language with fixed rules for writing
instructions that a computer can follow. This course uses **TypeScript**, and the TypeScript
lessons begin in [Day 5 - TypeScript](/learn/w1/d5/p1). Playwright also supports JavaScript,
Python, Java, and C#.

## Why teams choose Playwright

Before Playwright, many teams used **Selenium**, an older testing tool that is still widely used.
With Selenium, teams usually add several other tools to build a complete setup. Playwright includes
those tools itself:

| Feature | What it does |
|---|---|
| Automatic waiting | A web page can take a moment to load. Playwright waits for each element to be ready before it clicks or types, so you do not need to add waits yourself. |
| Assertions | An **assertion** is a check that compares the actual result with the expected result. Playwright includes its own assertions. |
| Test runner | A **test runner** is the program that starts your tests and reports which passed and which failed. Playwright includes one. |
| Screenshots and video | When a test fails, Playwright can save screenshots and a video, so that you can see what happened. |
| Codegen | **Codegen** records your clicks in a browser and writes the matching test code. You use it in [Day 4 - Fundamentals](/learn/w1/d4/p2). |

Selenium remains a good choice for many teams. Playwright is newer, and it was designed to include
the tools that teams had to add to Selenium separately.

## Other kinds of testing tools

Playwright tests applications through a web browser. Other kinds of testing need other tools. One
of them tests an **API**, the way one program asks another for data without a screen. For example,
when a banking app shows your balance, it asks the bank's server for the number through an API.

| Kind of testing | What it checks | Example tools |
|---|---|---|
| Web interface (UI) | The application in a browser, the way a user sees it | Playwright, Selenium, Cypress |
| API | The requests and responses that programs exchange, without a browser | Postman, REST Assured, Playwright |
| Performance | How the application behaves when many people use it at the same time | JMeter, k6, Gatling |
| Mobile apps | Apps that people install on a phone | Appium |

Playwright can make a desktop browser imitate a phone screen. This is called **mobile emulation**.
It is useful for testing websites on phone-sized screens, but it does not test apps that are
installed on a phone. For those, testers use a mobile testing tool such as Appium.

## Where the effort goes

Learning a testing tool is only part of the work. On a typical project, about half of the effort
goes into learning the application: what it does, how people use it, and what the correct result
is for each task. The other half goes into three skills together: the programming language,
finding elements reliably, and organizing the steps and checks of each test.

Knowing the application matters as much as knowing the tool.

## Explore the Playwright website

Open a new browser tab and follow these steps:

1. Go to **https://playwright.dev**.
2. Read the short description at the top of the home page, and the three features listed below it.
3. Select **Docs**, then **Writing tests**, and read the page quickly. The code on that page makes
   more sense after [Day 5 - Fundamentals](/learn/w1/d5/p2), where you write your first test.
4. Write down three features on the site that this lesson did not mention. You need them for
   [Practice](/learn/w1/d1/p4).
An automated test script runs 500 checks every night, and all of them pass. What does this tell you?

options: The application has no bugs in the areas that the checks cover.
The 500 checks that a person wrote produced their expected results.
No new bugs have appeared in the application since the last run.
checkpoint.explanation: Automation does not find bugs. Each check compares the actual result with an expected result that a person wrote in advance. A problem that nobody wrote a check for still passes, which is why people continue to test by hand as well.

blocks.text: According to this lesson, which two things do you need before you can automate a test?

options: A test runner and a tool that records video of every run
A known expected result and a way to find the element
A fast computer and a colleague who reviews your script line by line
checkpoint.explanation: Without a known expected result, the script has nothing to compare the actual result with. Without a reliable way to find the element, the script cannot click it, type into it, or read it. If either one is missing, the test stays manual.

blocks.text: Your manager asks you to automate tests for the company's Android app, which people install on their phones. Is Playwright the right tool?

options: Yes, because mobile support is one of the features that Playwright lists.
No. Playwright only imitates a phone screen inside a desktop browser.
No, because Playwright supports only websites that open on a desktop computer.
checkpoint.explanation: Playwright's mobile support is mobile emulation: a desktop browser imitates a phone screen. This is useful for testing websites on phone-sized screens. An app installed on a phone needs a mobile testing tool such as Appium.

blocks.text:
- **Software testing** checks that an application works as expected. A bug is a difference between the expected result and the actual result.
- **Automation does not find bugs.** It reports whether each check passed or failed, and a person decides what a failure means.
- Before you automate a test, you need a known expected result and a way to find the element.
- **Playwright** is a free, open-source tool that tests web applications through a browser, from the first step of a task to the last.
- About half of the effort on a project goes into learning the application. The other half goes into the language, finding elements, and organizing each test.

## What's next

Continue to [Practice](/learn/w1/d1/p4) for three short problems. In
[Day 2 - Fundamentals](/learn/w1/d2/p2), you set up your computer so that you can write and run
tests.

# Week 1 - Day 1 - Practice - Why automation, why Playwright

These three problems help you review what you learned in [Fundamentals](/learn/w1/d1/p2). You
answer each one in writing, using the lesson and the Playwright website.

| | |
|---|---|
| **Focus** | Three written problems that review this day's lesson, from Beginner level to Advanced. |
| **Prerequisites** | [Fundamentals](/learn/w1/d1/p2), including the Playwright website that it asks you to explore. |
| **Environment** | The editor on the right, where you write each answer as comments. |

## How the problems work

Each problem is marked with a level: **Beginner**, **Intermediate**, or **Advanced**. The problems
get harder in that order. Every practice page in this course uses the same three levels.

To answer a problem, select **Start this in the editor**. The editor on the right opens with a short
template. Write your answer on the lines that start with `//`. In TypeScript, a line that starts
with `//` is a **comment**: text for people to read, which the computer ignores.

When you finish a problem, select **Reveal solution** to compare your answer with a model answer.
Your answer does not need to match it word for word.

## When you are done

You now know what software testing is, what automation can and cannot do, and why teams choose
Playwright. In [Day 2 - Fundamentals](/learn/w1/d2/p2), you set up your computer so that you can
write and run tests.

problems.statement:
**What to build.** A short written answer about one test that you could run by hand. Choose any
application you use, such as a banking website or a shopping app, and one task in it, such as
signing in. Then answer these questions:

1. What are the steps, and what is the expected result?
2. Could Playwright automate this test? Use the two things from [Fundamentals](/learn/w1/d1/p2):
   a known expected result, and a way to find the element.
3. Which element on the page would the test need to find? Name a specific one, such as the
   **Login** button or the email field.

**Where.** In the editor, using the template.

**How you will know it worked.** You named a specific element, such as a button or a text field,
and not a whole page such as "the login page". If you cannot name one, the test may not be ready
to automate yet.
problems.solution:
**A model answer.** Your answer names a different test, which is expected.

> **The application and the task:** the course's banking website, and signing in.
>
> **The steps and the expected result:** open the login page, enter a valid email and password, and select **Login**. The expected result is that the account dashboard opens and shows your name.
>
> **Could Playwright automate it, and why?** Yes. The test has a known expected result, and every step uses an element that the test can find.
>
> **The element the test would need to find:** the **Login** button, and the two text fields for the email and the password.

**What makes a good answer** is naming a specific element, such as a button or a text field. An answer such as "automate the login page" is too general, because a test cannot click a whole page. It acts on one element at a time.

problems.statement:
**What to build.** A list of three Playwright features that [Fundamentals](/learn/w1/d1/p2) did
not describe, with one sentence for each that explains what the feature is for.

**Where.** Find the features on [playwright.dev](https://playwright.dev), and write your list in
the editor.

**How you will know it worked.** Your three features are different from each other, and each
sentence is in your own words.

> **Hint:** Look at the features on the home page, and at the headings in the menu of the
> **Docs** section. The lesson already describes automatic waiting, assertions, the test runner,
> screenshots and video, Codegen, and mobile emulation, so choose three others.
problems.solution:
**A model answer.** Three features from [playwright.dev](https://playwright.dev) that the lesson did not describe:

1. **Trace Viewer** records every step of a test run, with a picture of the page at each step. After a test fails, you can replay the run to see what went wrong.
2. **Test retries** run a failed test again, a set number of times, before reporting it as failed. This shows which tests fail only some of the time. You learn to configure retries in a later lesson.
3. **Parallel runs** start several tests at the same time instead of one after another, so that a large set of tests finishes sooner.

Other good choices include **UI Mode**, **component testing**, and **visual comparisons**.

**What makes a good answer** is that the three features do different things, and each sentence is in your own words.

problems.statement:
**What to build.** A short plan for one test in a kind of testing other than the web interface.
Choose API, performance, or mobile apps from the table in [Fundamentals](/learn/w1/d1/p2), and
describe one test in it. For example, a performance test could check what happens when 100
people sign in to a banking website at the same time. Then use the section *Where the effort goes*
in the same lesson to write down where most of the work for that test would go.

**Where.** In the editor, using the template.

**How you will know it worked.** You named a tool from the table that suits your test, and your
effort estimate describes your test in particular, not the general split.
problems.solution:
**A model answer.** This answer uses the performance example: checking what happens when 100 people sign in to the banking website at the same time.

> **The kind of testing, and a tool from the table:** performance testing, with k6.
>
> **The test, in one sentence:** 100 simulated users sign in at the same time, and every sign-in must finish within two seconds.
>
> **Where most of the work would go:** into learning the application. You need to know how signing in works behind the scenes, which test accounts you may use, and how fast the team expects a sign-in to be. Writing the test in the tool is the smaller part of the work.

**The point of this problem** is the balance of the effort. Learning the tool is the smaller part. Understanding the application, and what the correct result is for it, is most of the work.
